newsitem.title: INDIA: Rebel accused of Kashmir tourist abductions killed.
newsitem.headline: Rebel accused of Kashmir tourist abductions killed.

text.p: The leader of a guerrilla group which India has accused of involvement in the kidnappings of four Western tourists in Kashmir was killed in a shoot-out on Monday, the paramilitary Border Security Force (BSF) said.

"The chief of Harkat-ul-Ansar, Parvez Ahmad Gazi, a Pakistani national, was killed in an encounter with Border Security Force personnel at Gretabal, Nawakadal," P.K. Mishra, a senior BSF official, told Reuters.

Nawakadal is a neighbourhood of Srinagar, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir, mainly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state. Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have died in separatist violence in the state since 1990.
BSF guards also arrested the deputy chief and financial chief of Harkat-ul-Ansar after they were injured in the same shoot-out, Mishra said.

Indian officials say the mysterious Al-Faran guerrilla group that kidnapped the Western tourists in July 1995 is a front for Harkat-ul-Ansar, which operates from the one-third of Kashmir that Pakistan rules. India controls the rest.
Harkat-ul-Ansar, which denies any role in the kidnappings, has neither denied nor confirmed the death of their leader.

The tourists -- two Britons, an American and a German -- were abducted while trekking in the Himalayas. There has been no trace of the four for several months. The body of a fifth hostage, a Norwegian, was found beheaded in August 1995.

Pakistan denies Indian charges that it arms separatists in Kashmir, saying it provides only moral and diplomatic support to guerrillas in the region. India and Pakistan have fought two wars over Kashmir since independence from Britain in 1947.
Dozens of guerrilla groups seeking merger with Pakistan or independence have been fighting Indian security forces in Kashmir since 1990.
